claims.claim: Prototypes are early models of a product that simulate its design and functionality; teams build prototypes of varying degrees of fidelity, from low-fidelity paper prototypes to high-fidelity digital models that closely resemble the final product (Interaction Design Foundation working definition).
The fidelity of a prototype refers to how closely it matches the look-and-feel of the final system, and fidelity can vary in the areas of interactivity, visuals, and content (Nielsen Norman Group).

A high-fidelity prototype combines three ingredients: realistic visuals (graphics, spacing, and layout that look like a live system), real content (all the content that would appear in the final design, such as full articles and product-description text and images), and working interactions (clickable links and menus with automatic responses to the user's actions).

With high-fidelity interactivity and/or visuals, teams can test workflow, specific UI components, graphical elements such as affordance, page hierarchy, type legibility, image quality, and engagement; because high-fidelity prototypes often look like live software, test participants are more likely to behave realistically, as if interacting with a real system.

High-fidelity prototypes are computer-based and usually allow realistic (mouse-keyboard) user interactions; they take the design as close as possible to a true representation of the user interface and are assumed to be much more effective in collecting true human-performance data (e.g., time to complete a task) and in demonstrating actual products to clients, management, and others (Usability.gov).

The costs of high fidelity: building an interactive prototype is time consuming because every click target must be made to respond, and changes are harder than with a rough prototype; designers feel less wedded to low-fidelity designs, and once more time is invested in a design it is harder to give it up (Nielsen Norman Group).

IxDF lists the cons of high-fidelity prototypes as longer and costlier to create, users focusing on superficial details rather than content, designers resisting changes due to the investment of time and effort, and users mistaking the prototype for the finished product and forming biases; high fidelity is best for usability testing, evaluating the overall user experience, gathering detailed feedback on the final design, and demonstrating the product to stakeholders.

The social effect of polish: when a design looks very polished, it is easy for an executive to fall into the trap of saying 'this looks good, let's make it go live now,' and low-fidelity prototypes put less pressure on users, who are more likely to express negative reactions to rough designs (Nielsen Norman Group).

Prototypes are delivered along with prototype specifications — brief notes describing details that may be ambiguous, such as font size, spacing, click effects, and element states — to help developers, product managers, or clients understand the design during delivery; element specifications are indispensable in the development process (Nielsen Norman Group).

Research by Walker, Takayama, and Landay (2002), cited by Usability.gov, found low- and high-fidelity prototypes basically equivalent in finding usability issues, so high fidelity is not automatically a better problem-finder.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether high fidelity finds more usability problems than low fidelity: Usability.gov reports that both have been found basically equivalent in finding usability issues (Walker et al., 2002), while Nielsen Norman Group emphasizes that high-fidelity prototypes allow testing of workflow, specific UI components, page hierarchy, type legibility, image quality, and engagement, and IxDF states high-fidelity testing yields more accurate, applicable results.
positions: Walker, Takayama, and Landay 2002 (cited by Usability.gov): low- and high-fidelity prototypes are basically equivalent in finding usability issues.
Nielsen Norman Group: high-fidelity interactivity and visuals enable testing of workflow, specific components, page hierarchy, typography, and engagement.
IxDF: testing with high-fidelity prototypes yields more accurate, applicable results.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats high fidelity as the tool for testing the details (wording, spacing, feel) and realistic behavior — not as a generally better problem-finder — and states the equivalence finding honestly so readers do not overclaim high fidelity's power.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The polish of a high-fidelity prototype is double-edged: IxDF counts stakeholder engagement ('stakeholders experience the vision firsthand') among its pros, while Nielsen Norman Group warns that a polished design invites executives to ship it prematurely and that users hesitate less to criticize rough designs.
positions: IxDF: high fidelity is engaging; stakeholders experience the vision firsthand and can judge its alignment with user needs.
Nielsen Norman Group: polished designs tempt executives to say 'let's make it go live now,' and users are more likely to express negative reactions to low-fidelity designs.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both sides: the same realism that wins approval can suppress criticism, so teams should keep framing a high-fidelity prototype as a draft to be tested and changed.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Article by Kara Pernice, December 18, 2016. Supports: fidelity defined as how closely a prototype matches the look-and-feel of the final system, varying across interactivity, visuals, and content; the three high-fidelity ingredients (realistic visuals, real content, working interactions); the benefits of high fidelity (testing workflow, UI components, page hierarchy, type legibility, image quality, engagement; users behave realistically); the costs (interactive prototypes are time consuming to build and harder to change; designers feel less wedded to rough designs); and the social effect (polished designs tempt executives to ship; users more readily criticize rough designs).
